definition: Asavas and Arishtas are medicinal preparations made by soaking the drugs, either in powder form or in the form of decoction (Kashaya), in a solution of sugar or jaggery, as the case may be, for a specified period of time, during which it undergoes a process of fermentation generating alcohol, thus facilitating the extraction of the active principles contained in the drugs. The alcohol, so generated, also serves as a preservative.
method_of_preparation: For Arishta, the drugs are coarsely powdered and a Kashaya is prepared, strained and kept in a fermentation pot, vessel or barrel. Sugar, jaggery or honey according to the formula is dissolved, boiled, filtered and added. Prakshepa Dravyas are finely powdered and added, followed by cleaned Dhataki Pushpa when included. The vessel is sealed and kept under conditions intended to maintain a suitable fermentation temperature. After the specified period, completion of fermentation is examined; the fluid is decanted, strained and bottled. For Asava, the prescribed water with jaggery or sugar is boiled and cooled, placed in the fermentation vessel, and the fine drug powders are added; the remaining process is as for Arishta.
general_precautions: If fermentation is carried out in an earthen vessel, it should not be new. Water should first be boiled in the vessel. Absolute cleanliness is required. The inner surface of the fermentation vessel should be fumigated with Pippali Churna and smeared with ghee before the liquids are poured into it. In large-scale manufacture, wooden vats, porcelain jars or metal vessels may be used.
characteristics: The filtered Asava or Arishta should be clear without froth at the top. It should not become sour (cukra). The preparation has the characteristic of aromatic alcoholic odour.
preservation: Asavas and Arishtas can be kept indefinitely. They should be kept in well-stoppered bottles or jars.

definition: Arka is a liquid preparation obtained by distillation of certain liquids or drugs soaked in water using the Arkayantra or any convenient modern distillation apparatus.
method_of_preparation: The drugs are cleaned and coarsely powdered. Water is added for soaking and the drugs are kept overnight. The following morning the material is placed in the Arka yantra with the remaining water and boiled. Vapour is condensed and collected in a receiver. The initial vapour, consisting mainly of steam, and the last portion, which may not contain therapeutically essential substances, are discarded. The intermediate fractions containing active ingredients may be mixed to ensure uniformity.
characteristics: Arka is a suspension of the distillate in water having slight turbidity and colour according to the nature of the drugs used and smell of the predominant drug.

definition: Avaleha or Lehya is a semi-solid preparation of drugs, prepared with addition of jaggery, sugar or sugar-candy and boiled with prescribed drug juice or decoction. They are also known as Modaka, Guda, Khanda, Rasayana, Leha etc.
method_of_preparation: These preparations generally have Kashaya or other liquids, jaggery, sugar or sugar-candy, powders or pulps of certain drugs, and ghee or oil and honey. Jaggery, sugar or sugar-candy is dissolved in the liquid and strained. The solution is boiled over moderate fire. When the Paka is thready (tantuvat) between two fingers or sinks in water without getting easily dissolved, it is removed from the fire. Fine drug powders are added in small quantities with continuous vigorous stirring. Ghee or oil, if mentioned, is added while hot and mixed well. Honey, if mentioned, is added after cooling.
characteristics: The Lehya should neither be hard nor a thick fluid. When drug pulp and ghee or oil are present, it can be rolled between the fingers. Growth of fungus or fermentation are signs of deterioration. When metals are mentioned, their bhasmas are used. For drugs such as Bhallataka, purified drugs alone are included. Colour and smell depend on the drugs used.
preservation: Lehya should be kept in glass or porcelain jars, or in a non-reactive metal container. Normally, Lehyas should be used within one year.

definition: Certain drugs or combinations of drugs are made into coarse powder (Yavakuta) and kept for preparation of Kashaya. Such powders are called Kwatha Churna.
method_of_preparation: Drugs are cleaned and dried. They are coarsely powdered (Yavakuta), weighed as per formula, and then mixed well.
characteristics: Kwatha Churnas retain potency for one year. They are also called Shrita, Niryuhha and Kashaya. Kwatha Churna can be used for preparing Kashaya, Hima, Phanta, etc.
preservation: They should be kept in an air-tight container.

definition: Guggulu is an exudate (Niryasa) obtained from the plant Commiphora mukul. Preparations having the exudate as the main effective ingredient are known as Guggulu. Five different varieties are described in the texts; Mahiṣākṣa and Kanaka Guggulu are usually preferred for medicinal preparations.
method_of_preparation: The category describes Shodhana of Guggulu. Foreign matter such as sand and glass is removed, the Guggulu is broken into small pieces, bundled in cloth and boiled in a Dola Yantra containing a specified fluid such as Gomutra, Triphala Kashaya, Vasapatra Kashaya, Vasapatra Svarasa, Nirgundi-patra Svarasa with Haridra Churna, or Dugdha. Boiling continues until the Guggulu becomes soft. The mass is then processed to remove remaining impurities, fried with ghee and ground. An alternative method suspends the bundle in the specified fluid until the Guggulu passes into the fluid; the filtered fluid is boiled to form a mass, dried and pounded with ghee until waxy.
characteristics: Shodhita Guggulu is soft, waxy and brown in colour. Characteristics of Guggulu preparations vary depending on the other ingredients added.
preservation: It should be kept in glass or porcelain jars free from moisture and stored in a cool place. Potency is maintained for two years when prepared with ingredients of plant origin and indefinitely when prepared with metals and minerals.

definition: Ghritas are preparations in which ghee is boiled with prescribed Kashayas (decoctions) and Kalkas of drugs according to the formula. This process ensures absorption of the active therapeutic principles of the ingredients used.
method_of_preparation: There are generally three essential components for preparation of Sneha (Ghrita or Taila): Drava, a liquid such as Kashaya, Svarasa, Dugdha or Mastu; Kalka, a fine paste of the drugs; and Sneha Dravya, such as Ghrita or Murchita Ghrita. Unless otherwise stated, one part Kalka, four parts Sneha and sixteen parts Drava are used, subject to stated exceptions. Kalka and Drava are mixed, Sneha is added, and the mixture is boiled on mild fire with continuous stirring. The Drava Dravyas may be added successively as earlier liquids evaporate. The category describes three stages of Paka: Mridu, Madhyama and Khara; further heating produces Dagdha Paka, making the Sneha unfit for use.
general_precautions: Boiling should begin and end on mild fire. The Kalka should be stirred so that it does not adhere to the vessel. When Lavanas and Ksharas are used, they are added to the Sneha and then strained.
characteristics: Ghrita generally solidifies when cooled and has the colour, odour and taste of the drugs used.
preservation: Ghritas are preserved in glass, polythene or aluminium containers. Ghrita preparations for internal use keep their potency for about sixteen months.

definition: Churna is a fine powder of drug or drugs.
method_of_preparation: Drugs mentioned in the Yoga are cleaned and dried properly, finely powdered and sieved. Where there are several drugs, they are separately powdered, sieved and weighed before being mixed. In industry, drugs may be cleaned, dried and powdered together using disintegrators and mechanical sifters. Salt, sugar and camphor are separately powdered and mixed at the end. Asafoetida and salt may be roasted before powdering. Drugs intended to be used fresh may be made into a paste, dried and added.
characteristics: The powder is fine, of at least 80-mesh sieve. It should not adhere together or become moist. The finer the powder, the better is its therapeutic value.
preservation: Churnas retain potency for one year and should be kept in air-tight containers.

definition: Tailas are preparations in which Taila is boiled with prescribed Kashayas (decoction) and Kalkas of drugs according to the formula. This process ensures absorption of the active therapeutic properties of the ingredients used.
method_of_preparation: There are generally three essential components for preparation of Sneha (Ghrita or Taila): Drava, a liquid such as Kashaya, Svarasa, Dugdha or Mastu; Kalka, a fine paste of the drugs; and Sneha Dravya, such as Taila or Murchita Taila. Unless otherwise stated, one part Kalka, four parts Sneha and sixteen parts Drava are used, subject to stated exceptions. Kalka and Drava are mixed, Sneha is added, and the mixture is boiled on mild fire with continuous stirring. The Drava Dravyas may be added successively as earlier liquids evaporate. The category describes Mridu, Madhyama and Khara Paka, with further heating producing Dagdha Paka and making the Sneha unfit for use.
general_precautions: Boiling should begin and end on mild fire. The Kalka should be stirred so that it does not adhere to the vessel. When Lavanas and Ksharas are used, they are added to the Sneha and then strained.
characteristics: Taila generally has the colour, odour and taste of the drugs used and the consistency of oil. When considerable milk is used, the oil becomes thick due to Ghrita and may condense further in cold weather.
preservation: Tailas are preserved in glass, polythene or aluminium containers. Preparations for internal use keep their potency for about sixteen months.

definition: Dravakas are liquid preparations obtained from Lavanas and Ksharas.
method_of_preparation: Dravakas are prepared with Lavanas and Ksharas by Tiryakpatana (distillation) process with or without addition of fluids.
preservation: They are preserved in glass-stoppered bottles. These preparations do not deteriorate by lapse of time.

source_note: The supplied AFI text places the formulation list immediately after the category heading; no separate category-level definition, general preparation, characteristics or preservation text was located in this section.

definition: Medicines in the form of a paste used for external application are called Lepas.
method_of_preparation: The drugs are made into a fine powder. Before use on the body, it is mixed with the liquid or other medium indicated in each preparation and made into a soft paste. Water, cow's urine, oil and ghee are some of the media used.
preservation: Vegetable Lepa Churna preserve their potency for 30 days if kept in air-tight containers. Mineral and metallic preparations last indefinitely.

definition: Medicines prepared in the form of tablet or pills are known as Vati and Gutika. These are made of one or more drugs of plant, animal or mineral origin.
method_of_preparation: Plant drugs are dried and made into fine powders separately. Minerals are made into Bhasma or Sindura unless otherwise mentioned. Where Parada and Gandhaka are mentioned, Kajjali is made first and other drugs are added according to the formula. The ingredients are ground in a Khalva with prescribed fluids. Sugandha Dravyas are added near the final stage. The mass is ready for pill-making when it does not stick to the fingers when rolled. Pills may be dried in shade or sun as specified. Where sugar or jaggery is used, its Paka is prepared on mild fire, the powders are added and mixed briskly, and Vatakas are rolled while warm and dried in shade.
characteristics: Pills made of plant drugs can be used for two years when kept in air-tight containers; pills containing minerals can be used indefinitely. Pills and Vatis should retain their original colour, smell, taste and form.
preservation: When sugar, salt or Kshara is an ingredient, the pills should be kept away from moisture. Air-tight containers are specified for preservation.

definition: Medicines used externally for the eye come under the category of Varti, Netrabindu and Anjana.
method_of_preparation: Vartis are made by grinding fine powders of the drugs with the fluids in the formula to form a soft paste. This is made into thin sticks of about 2 centimetres in length and dried in shade. Netrabindu is prepared by dissolving the specified drugs in water or Kashaya and used as eye drops. Anjanas are very fine semisolids of drugs applied with Netra Shalaka.
characteristics: Colour and smell depend on the drugs used.
preservation: These can be preserved for one year if kept in an air-tight container. Formulations in which minerals are used are preserved indefinitely.

definition: Sattva is water extractable solid substance collected from a drug.
method_of_preparation: The drug is cut into small pieces, macerated in water and kept overnight. It is then strained through cloth and the solid matter is allowed to settle. The supernatant liquid is decanted and the Sattva is washed by repeating the process with water and decanting. The sedimented Sattva is allowed to dry and powdered.
characteristics: The colour varies from drug to drug.
preservation: It can be preserved in a closed container.

method_of_preparation: Drugs of mineral and metallic origin (Rasauṣadhi) are well mixed in fine powder form and usually placed in a glass flask (Kachakupi) one-third full. Clay-smeared pieces of cloth are pasted around the bottle in seven consecutive layers. After drying, the flask is buried in a Valukayantra up to the neck and heated gradually in three stages of Agni: Mridvagni, Madhyamagni and Tikshnagni for a specified period. A red-hot iron rod is inserted through the opening and used to stir from time to time so that subliming sulphur does not choke the opening.
general_precautions: The category gives completion tests and cautions that the flask opening should not become choked by subliming sulphur because pressure may break the flask. After completion and cooling, the flask is handled carefully and the deposited Sindura is collected without mixing glass fragments.
characteristics: The colour of the Rasa preparation depends on the drugs used; generally preparations are red, yellow or dark.
preservation: They have to be kept in well-stoppered bottles and keep their potency indefinitely.

definition: Parpati is a Rasa preparation. The name is derived from the method by which flakes of the compound are obtained.
method_of_preparation: Kajjali is prepared first with purified mercury (Parada) and sulphur (Gandhaka). Other drugs are added one by one and mixed by trituration in a Khalva. The powder is put in an iron vessel over fire in the Sikatayantra. A shallow pit in fresh cow dung is prepared and a Kadali or Eranda leaf is spread over it. When the medicine melts and becomes liquid it is poured onto the leaf, another leaf is placed over it, and fresh cow dung is spread and gently pressed. After cooling, the flakes are collected and powdered.
preservation: They preserve their potency indefinitely and are kept in glass bottles.

definition: Pishti are prepared by triturating the drug with the specified liquids and exposing it to sun or moonlight. These are termed Anagnitapta Bhasma (bhasma prepared without the medium of fire).
method_of_preparation: After purification (Shodhana), the drug is put in a Khalva and triturated generally with rose water unless otherwise mentioned. It is triturated with the liquid for a day and dried in the sun for another day. This is generally continued for seven days or more until a fine Pishti in powder form is obtained.
characteristics: Depending upon the colour of the drug, Pishtis are of different colours. They are as fine as Bhasma and have the characteristics of Bhasma.
preservation: They preserve their potency indefinitely and are stored in glass-stoppered bottles.

definition: Powder of a substance obtained by calcination is called Bhasma. In this section, it is applied to metals, minerals and animal products which are, by special processes, calcined in closed crucibles in pits and with cow dung cakes (Puta).
method_of_preparation: Bhasmas are prepared from purified minerals, metals, and marine and animal products. The first stage is Shodhana, which may be Samanya Shodhana or Vishesha Shodhana. The second stage is Marana: the purified drug is ground in a Khalva with specified plant juices or Kashayas, small cakes (Chakrikas) are prepared, dried, placed in a Sharava, covered and sealed with clay-smeared cloth in seven layers, and subjected to the prescribed Puta process. The process is repeated as prescribed or until the proper fineness and quality are obtained.
general_precautions: The category describes different Puta sizes and heat requirements, including Maha Puta, Gaja Puta, Varaha Puta, Kukuta Puta, Kapota Puta and Bhanda Puta.
characteristics: Properly prepared Bhasma should have no metallic lustre (Nishchandrika), be fine enough to enter finger lines (Rekha Purita), float on still water (Varitaram), and not revert to the original state (Apunarbhava). Depending on the drugs, Bhasmas may be yellowish, black, white, grey, reddish black or red, and have no characteristic taste.
preservation: Bhasmas are preserved in air-tight glass or earthen containers and maintain their potency indefinitely.

definition: These are preparations containing Shodhita Mandura along with other drugs.
method_of_preparation: Mandura is purified by a special method and boiled in Gomutra until it becomes a Rasakriya (paste). The powders mentioned in the Yogas are added and stirred well. While warm, Vatakas are prepared. It can also be kept in powder form.
characteristics: These emit a strong smell of Gomutra and are dark in colour.
preservation: They preserve their potency indefinitely and should be kept away from moisture.

definition: Preparations containing mineral drugs as main ingredients are called Rasa Yogas. They may be in pill form. They are mixed and triturated together.
method_of_preparation: Drugs such as Abhraka, Makshika, Svarna, Rajata, Tamra and Kansya are used only in Bhasma form. Drugs such as Gandhaka and Manahshila are used in purified form. Where Rasa and Gandhaka are drugs, Kajjali is prepared first and then other drugs are added in small quantities and ground in the Khalva and mixed well. Bhavana with the prescribed Svarasa, Kashaya etc. is given for the prescribed period.
characteristics: The colour and smell depend on the drugs in the Yogas.
preservation: They keep their potency indefinitely, unless otherwise prescribed.

definition: Lauha Kalpas are preparations of Lauha Bhasma as the main ingredient added to other drugs.
method_of_preparation: The drugs are reduced to fine powder and mixed with Lauha Bhasma. Bhavana is given with prescribed liquids if mentioned.
characteristics: The powder should be very fine and the Bhasma used should be well prepared.
preservation: When well protected from moisture and heat, they keep their potency for a period of two years. Preparations containing mercury or its compounds keep their potency indefinitely.
